slides.narration: Welcome to Probability. Will you get a six on your next throw in Ludo? Will a coin show heads? Probability measures how likely something is, with a number from zero to one. Zero means impossible, one means certain, and one half means an even chance. In this part we learn how to calculate that number.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. This chapter uses the theoretical, or classical, idea of probability. We do not need to toss a coin a thousand times; we reason from the outcomes, as long as they are equally likely.

slides.heading: Experiments and outcomes
slides.body_md: An **experiment** has well-defined **outcomes**. An **event** is a set of outcomes, for example "an even number" when a die is thrown.

visual.alt: Table of experiments: tossing a coin has 2 outcomes, throwing a die 6, drawing a disc numbered 1 to 20 has 20, and drawing a card from a deck 52.
visual.caption: List the outcomes before counting.

slides.narration: Tossing a coin, throwing a die and drawing a card are experiments. Each has a list of possible outcomes: two for a coin, six for a die, fifty two for a deck of cards. An event is any collection of outcomes that we are interested in, like getting an even number, which is the outcomes two, four and six.

slides.heading: Equally likely outcomes
slides.body_md: The classical formula works only when every outcome has the **same chance**: a fair coin, a fair die, a well-shuffled deck, balls of the same size.

slides.narration: Look at the two spinners. On the left, the four sectors are equal, so each colour is equally likely. On the right, the blue sector is half the circle, so blue is far more likely than red. Our formula needs equally likely outcomes. That is why questions say a fair die, a well-shuffled deck, or balls of the same size.

slides.heading: Theoretical probability
slides.body_md: For equally likely outcomes,

visual.alt: Table of events for one die: a prime number has favourable outcomes 2, 3 and 5, probability one half; greater than 4 has 5 and 6, one third; a multiple of 7 has none, probability 0; less than 7 has all six, probability 1.
visual.caption: $P(E) = \dfrac{\text{favourable}}{\text{total}}$.

math: P(E) = \frac{\text{number of outcomes favourable to } E}{\text{total number of possible outcomes}}
slides.narration: Here is the definition. Count the outcomes that make the event happen, the favourable ones. Divide by the total number of outcomes. For a die, three of the six faces are prime, so the probability of a prime is three sixths, one half. Always reduce the fraction at the end.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: one die
slides.body_md: A fair die is thrown once. Find the probability of getting (a) a prime number (b) a number greater than $4$ (c) a multiple of $7$.
bullets: **(c)** No face is a multiple of $7$: $P = 0$, an **impossible** event.

visual.alt: Table of events for one die: a prime number has favourable outcomes 2, 3 and 5, probability one half; greater than 4 has 5 and 6, one third; a multiple of 7 has none, probability 0; less than 7 has all six, probability 1.
visual.caption: $P(E) = \dfrac{\text{favourable}}{\text{total}}$.

slides.narration: List the six outcomes first. Then count. For primes, be careful: one is not a prime number, so only two, three and five count. Greater than four means five and six only. And no face is a multiple of seven, so that event is impossible, with probability zero. Write each answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.

slides.heading: Quick check: one die
slides.body_md: Count the favourable faces.
slides.narration: Which faces are less than three? How many faces are there in all?

slides.body_md: Favourable outcomes are between $0$ and $n$, so $0 \le P(E) \le 1$. An **impossible** event has $P = 0$; a **sure** event has $P = 1$.

visual.caption: Every probability lies between $0$ (impossible) and $1$ (certain).

slides.narration: Since the number of favourable outcomes is between zero and the total, every probability lies between zero and one. Zero means the event can never happen. One means it always happens, like getting a number up to six on a die. An answer greater than one, or negative, is a sure sign of a mistake.

slides.heading: Complementary events
slides.body_md: The event "not $E$" happens exactly when $E$ does not. Together they cover every outcome, with no overlap:

visual.alt: Table of complementary events: a 6 on a die has probability one sixth and its complement five sixths; a multiple of 3 among discs 1 to 20 has three tenths and its complement seven tenths; rain tomorrow 0.08 and no rain 0.92; each pair sums to 1.
visual.caption: $P(E) + P(\text{not } E) = 1$.

slides.narration: Every outcome either belongs to E or to not E, never both. So their probabilities add up to one. This gives a powerful shortcut: when it is easier to count what you do not want, find that probability and subtract it from one. Questions with the words not, at least, or at most often use this idea.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: using the complement
slides.body_md: (a) In Ludo, find the probability of **not** getting a $6$. (b) Discs numbered $1$ to $20$ are in a box; find the probability that the disc drawn is **not** a multiple of $3$.

visual.alt: Table of complementary events: a 6 on a die has probability one sixth and its complement five sixths; a multiple of 3 among discs 1 to 20 has three tenths and its complement seven tenths; rain tomorrow 0.08 and no rain 0.92; each pair sums to 1.
visual.caption: $P(E) + P(\text{not } E) = 1$.

slides.narration: In the first part, counting the five faces that are not six is easy too, but the complement is quicker. In the second part, the multiples of three are only six numbers, while the others are fourteen. Count the smaller set and subtract from one: seven tenths. Both ways give the same answer.

slides.heading: Quick check: complement
slides.body_md: Subtract from $1$.
slides.narration: If the probability of an event is zero point three five, what is left for the event not happening?

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a bag of balls
slides.body_md: A bag has $5$ red, $3$ blue and $2$ green balls of the same size. One ball is drawn at random. Find $P(\text{red})$, $P(\text{blue})$ and $P(\text{not green})$.

visual.caption: Ten equally likely balls.

slides.narration: Each ball is equally likely to be picked, because they are the same size. So the total is ten. Red has five of the ten, one half. Blue has three tenths. For not green, either count the eight non-green balls or subtract green from one: four fifths. Never divide one colour by another colour.

slides.heading: All the elementary events add up to 1
slides.body_md: Each single outcome (or each colour in a bag) is an **elementary event**. Their probabilities always add to $1$.

visual.alt: Table for the bag: red 5 balls, probability one half; blue 3, three tenths; green 2, one fifth; the probabilities add to 1.
visual.caption: Probabilities of all elementary events add up to $1$.

slides.narration: For the bag, red, blue and green have probabilities one half, three tenths and one fifth. Add them: five tenths, three tenths and two tenths make one. This is always true for elementary events, and it is a quick check on your work. If your probabilities add to more than one, something was counted twice.

slides.heading: Quick check: impossible event
slides.body_md: What is the smallest possible probability?
slides.narration: If no outcome is favourable, what is the numerator of the fraction?

slides.heading: Summary

visual.alt: Summary table of part one: theoretical probability is favourable over total for equally likely outcomes; it lies between 0 and 1; impossible events have 0 and sure events 1; the complement is 1 minus P of E; elementary events add to 1.
visual.caption: Five rules of probability.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. List the equally likely outcomes, count the favourable ones, and divide. Every probability is between zero and one. Impossible events have zero and sure events one. The complement rule, one minus P of E, is a quick way to handle not and at least questions.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **1-mark items:** give the fraction in lowest terms
**2-mark items:** total outcomes 1 + favourable count and answer 1
**Mistake:** treating unequal outcomes as equally likely
slides.narration: Write the total number of outcomes and the favourable outcomes separately; each line can earn a mark. List them when the numbers are small. Reduce the fraction. Before moving on, check that your answer is between zero and one, and for complements, that the two probabilities add to one.

decks.title: Probability — Part 2: Coins, dice, cards and discs
goals: List outcomes for two and three coins
Use the 36 outcomes of two dice
Find probabilities with a deck of 52 cards
Solve problems on numbered discs, tickets and bags

slides.heading: Probability, Part 2: Coins, dice, cards and discs
slides.body_md: Two dice give $36$ equally likely outcomes, not $11$.

visual.alt: Six by six table of sums for two dice: rows give the first die from 1 to 6, columns the second die from 1 to 6, and each cell the sum, from 2 in the top left corner to 12 in the bottom right; each of the 36 cells is equally likely.
visual.caption: Two dice: $36$ equally likely outcomes. Sum $7$ appears $6$ times; sums $2$ and $12$ once each.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Now the experiments get richer: several coins, two dice, a full deck of cards. The key skill is to list or count the equally likely outcomes correctly. Look at this table of two dice: thirty six cells, each equally likely. The sum seven appears six times, but the sum twelve only once.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: List outcomes of **two and three coins**
Use the **$6 \times 6$ table** for two dice
Use the structure of a **deck of 52 cards**
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. Every question still uses the same formula, favourable over total. What changes is how carefully we count. Tables and tree diagrams make the counting reliable.

slides.heading: Two and three coins
slides.body_md: Each coin doubles the number of outcomes: one coin $2$, two coins $4$, three coins $8$. A tree diagram lists them all.

visual.alt: Tree diagram for tossing three coins: each coin branches into heads or tails, giving 2, then 4, then 8 outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH and TTT.
visual.caption: Three coins: $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ equally likely outcomes.

slides.narration: With two coins, the outcomes are head head, head tail, tail head and tail tail. Head tail and tail head are different outcomes, because the coins are different. With three coins there are eight outcomes. The tree shows how each coin splits every branch into two. Counting heads is then easy.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: coins
slides.body_md: (a) Two coins are tossed: find $P(\text{at least one head})$. (b) Three coins are tossed: find $P(\text{exactly two heads})$.
bullets: **(a)** Outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT. At least one head: HH, HT, TH. $P = \dfrac34$.
**(b)** Exactly two heads: HHT, HTH, THH. $P = \dfrac38$.
**Trap —** "$0, 1, 2$ heads" are not equally likely, so $\dfrac13$ is wrong.

visual.alt: Tree diagram for tossing three coins: each coin branches into heads or tails, giving 2, then 4, then 8 outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH and TTT.
visual.caption: Three coins: $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ equally likely outcomes.

slides.narration: At least one head means one or two heads, which is everything except tail tail. So the complement gives three quarters quickly. For three coins, read the tree: three outcomes have exactly two heads, out of eight. A common trap is to think zero, one and two heads are equally likely. They are not.

slides.heading: Quick check: two coins
slides.body_md: List all four outcomes.
slides.narration: Write the four outcomes. Which of them contain at least one tail?

slides.heading: Two dice: the 6 by 6 table
slides.body_md: Each of the $6$ results of the first die pairs with each of the $6$ of the second: $36$ equally likely ordered pairs. $(2, 5)$ and $(5, 2)$ are different outcomes.

visual.alt: Six by six table of sums for two dice: rows give the first die from 1 to 6, columns the second die from 1 to 6, and each cell the sum, from 2 in the top left corner to 12 in the bottom right; each of the 36 cells is equally likely.
visual.caption: Two dice: $36$ equally likely outcomes. Sum $7$ appears $6$ times; sums $2$ and $12$ once each.

slides.narration: For two dice, use a six by six table. Rows are the first die, columns the second. Each cell is one outcome, and all thirty six are equally likely. Notice that two then five and five then two are different cells. Fill in the sums, or the products, and simply count the cells you need.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: sums of two dice
slides.body_md: Two dice are thrown. Find the probability that (a) the sum is $8$ (b) both show the same number (c) the sum is at least $10$.
bullets: **Check —** In the table, sum $8$ lies on one diagonal of $5$ cells.

visual.alt: Six by six table of sums for two dice: rows give the first die from 1 to 6, columns the second die from 1 to 6, and each cell the sum, from 2 in the top left corner to 12 in the bottom right; each of the 36 cells is equally likely.
visual.caption: Two dice: $36$ equally likely outcomes. Sum $7$ appears $6$ times; sums $2$ and $12$ once each.

slides.narration: Use the table. The sum eight appears on a diagonal of five cells, so five thirty-sixths. Doublets are the six cells on the main diagonal, one sixth. For at least ten, count sums ten, eleven and twelve: three, two and one cells, six in all, so again one sixth.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: products of two dice
slides.body_md: Two dice are thrown. Find the probability that the product of the numbers is (a) even (b) a perfect square.
bullets: **(a)** The product is odd only if both are odd: $3 \times 3 = 9$ outcomes. $P(\text{even}) = 1 - \dfrac{9}{36} = \dfrac34$.
**Tip —** Use the complement when the "bad" case is easier.

visual.alt: Table of products of two dice that are perfect squares: 1 from one pair, 4 from three pairs, 9 from one pair, and 16, 25 and 36 from one pair each, eight outcomes in all.
visual.caption: $8$ of $36$ products are perfect squares.

slides.narration: For an even product, it is easier to count the odd products: both dice must be odd, three choices each, nine outcomes. So the even product has probability one minus nine thirty-sixths, three quarters. For perfect squares, list them carefully: four can come from one and four, four and one, or two and two. Eight outcomes in all.

slides.heading: Quick check: two dice
slides.body_md: Count cells in the $6 \times 6$ table.
slides.narration: How many cells in the table have the sum seven? How many cells are there in all?

slides.heading: A deck of 52 cards
slides.body_md: $4$ suits of $13$: spades and clubs (black), hearts and diamonds (red). Each suit: ace, $2$–$10$, jack, queen, king. **Face cards:** J, Q, K — $12$ in all.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: one card

sections.heading: 1. Experiments, outcomes and events
sections.body_md:
An **experiment** (tossing a coin, throwing a die, drawing a card) has a set of possible **outcomes**. An **event** is a collection of outcomes, e.g. "an even number" $= \{2, 4, 6\}$ for a die. An **elementary event** has exactly one outcome.

Outcomes are **equally likely** when each has the same chance: a fair coin or die, a well-shuffled deck, balls of the same size drawn without looking. The classical definition of probability needs equally likely outcomes.

key_terms.definition_md: A possible result of an experiment.
A collection of outcomes of an experiment.
Every outcome has the same chance of occurring.

sections.heading: 2. Theoretical (classical) probability
sections.body_md:
For an experiment with equally likely outcomes,

$$P(E) = \frac{\text{number of outcomes favourable to } E}{\text{total number of possible outcomes}}.$$

- $0 \le P(E) \le 1$; an **impossible** event has $P = 0$, a **sure** event $P = 1$.
- The probabilities of all elementary events add up to $1$.

*Example:* one die: $P(\text{prime}) = \dfrac36 = \dfrac12$; $P(\text{greater than } 4) = \dfrac13$; $P(\text{multiple of } 7) = 0$.

key_terms.definition_md: An event with no favourable outcomes; probability $0$.
An event containing every outcome; probability $1$.

sections.heading: 3. Complementary events
sections.body_md:
"Not $E$" happens exactly when $E$ does not. So

$$P(E) + P(\text{not } E) = 1, \qquad P(\text{not } E) = 1 - P(E).$$

Use it for "not", "at least one", "at most": e.g. at least one head with two coins $= 1 - P(\text{TT}) = \dfrac34$; at least one 6 with two dice $= 1 - \dfrac{25}{36} = \dfrac{11}{36}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The event "not $E$", consisting of all outcomes not in $E$.

visual.alt: Table of complementary events: a 6 on a die has probability one sixth and its complement five sixths; a multiple of 3 among discs 1 to 20 has three tenths and its complement seven tenths; rain tomorrow 0.08 and no rain 0.92; each pair sums to 1.
visual.caption: $P(E) + P(\text{not } E) = 1$.

sections.heading: 4. Coins and dice
sections.body_md:
- **Coins:** $n$ coins give $2^n$ outcomes: $2$, $4$, $8$. HT and TH are different. A tree diagram lists them.
- **One die:** $6$ outcomes.
- **Two dice:** $36$ ordered pairs $(a, b)$; use a $6 \times 6$ table. Sums are **not** equally likely: sum $7$ in $6$ ways, sums $2$ and $12$ in $1$ way each.

*Examples:* $P(\text{sum } 8) = \dfrac{5}{36}$; $P(\text{doublet}) = \dfrac16$; $P(\text{even product}) = \dfrac34$; three coins, $P(\text{exactly two heads}) = \dfrac38$.

key_terms.definition_md: The same number on both dice.

sections.heading: 5. Playing cards
sections.body_md:
A deck has $52$ cards in $4$ suits of $13$: spades ♠ and clubs ♣ (black), hearts ♥ and diamonds ♦ (red). Each suit has an ace, $2$–$10$, and the **face cards** jack, queen, king. So: $26$ red, $26$ black, $12$ face cards, $4$ of each rank.

- "$A$ or $B$": count each card once (spade or ace: $13 + 3 = 16$).
- Cards removed: recount the total first (no jacks: $48$ cards).

*Examples:* $P(\text{red king}) = \dfrac{1}{26}$; $P(\text{face card}) = \dfrac{3}{13}$; $P(\text{neither heart nor king}) = \dfrac{36}{52} = \dfrac{9}{13}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Jack, queen and king — 12 in a deck.

sections.heading: 6. Discs, tickets and bags
sections.body_md:
- **Discs or tickets numbered $a$ to $b$:** $b - a + 1$ outcomes. List multiples, squares or primes explicitly ($1$ is not prime). "Divisible by both $4$ and $6$" means divisible by $12$.
- **Bags:** each ball is an outcome (balls of the same size). $P(\text{colour}) = \dfrac{\text{balls of that colour}}{\text{total balls}}$. Adding or removing balls changes the total; unknown numbers lead to a simple equation.

*Examples:* discs $1$–$50$: $P(\text{square}) = \dfrac{7}{50}$; bag of $6$ red and $b$ blue with $P(\text{blue}) = \dfrac35$ gives $b = 9$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *1 mark:* the probability as a fraction in lowest terms.
- *2–3 marks:* total outcomes 1; favourable outcomes (listed or counted) 1 per part; answer 1.

**Common mistakes**
1. Outcomes not equally likely (6 or not 6; sums of two dice).
2. $(2, 5)$ and $(5, 2)$ counted as one.
3. Double counting in "or" questions.
4. Total not updated after removing cards or adding balls.
5. $1$ counted as a prime; aces counted as face cards.
6. Answers greater than $1$ or not reduced.

An event with exactly one outcome.

cards.back_md: The two results are not equally likely; $P(6) = \dfrac16$.
No — it must lie between $0$ and $1$.

cards.back_md: No — larger sectors are more likely.

cards.back_md: Only when both numbers are odd: $9$ of $36$.

cards.front_md: Spade or ace: how many cards?
"Divisible by both 4 and 6" means divisible by…

questions.stem_md: The probability of an impossible event is
questions.solution_md: An impossible event has no favourable outcomes: $P = \dfrac{0}{n} = 0$. A probability is never negative.

questions.stem_md: Which of these cannot be the probability of an event?
questions.solution_md: For every event, $0 \le P(E) \le 1$. $1.2 > 1$, so it cannot be a probability.

questions.stem_md: If $P(E) = 0.35$, then $P(\text{not } E)$ is
A die is thrown once. The probability of getting a number less than 3 is
questions.solution_md: Favourable: $1, 2$ — two outcomes out of six. $P = \dfrac26 = \dfrac13$. Option (a) counts $1, 2, 3$ ("3 or less").

questions.stem_md: A die is thrown once. The probability of getting a prime number is
questions.solution_md: Primes on a die: $2, 3, 5$. $P = \dfrac36 = \dfrac12$. Option (b) wrongly counts $1$ as a prime.

questions.stem_md: A coin is tossed twice. The probability of getting at least one tail is
questions.solution_md: Outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. At least one tail: HT, TH, TT. $P = \dfrac34$. Option (a) treats "two heads, one head, no head" as three equally likely outcomes, which they are not.

questions.stem_md: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. The probability that it is a red king is
questions.solution_md: There are $2$ red kings (hearts, diamonds). $P = \dfrac{2}{52} = \dfrac{1}{26}$. Option (d) counts all four kings.

questions.stem_md: A card is drawn at random from a deck of 52 cards. The probability that it is a face card is
questions.solution_md: Face cards are the jack, queen and king of each suit: $12$. $P = \dfrac{12}{52} = \dfrac{3}{13}$. Option (a) includes the aces.

questions.stem_md: A bag has 4 red and 6 white balls. One ball is drawn at random. The probability that it is white is
questions.solution_md: $P(\text{white}) = \dfrac{6}{10} = \dfrac35$. Option (d) divides white by red — and is more than $1$, so it cannot be a probability.

questions.stem_md: Discs numbered 1 to 25 are put in a box and one is drawn at random. The probability that its number is a multiple of 5 is
questions.solution_md: Multiples of $5$: $5, 10, 15, 20, 25$ — five of them. $P = \dfrac{5}{25} = \dfrac15$. Option (d) forgets $25$.

questions.stem_md: Two dice are thrown together. The probability that the sum of the numbers is 7 is
questions.solution_md: $36$ equally likely outcomes; sum $7$: $(1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1)$ — six. $P = \dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac16$. Option (a) wrongly treats the eleven sums $2$–$12$ as equally likely.

questions.stem_md: Two dice are thrown together. The probability of getting the same number on both (a doublet) is
questions.solution_md: Doublets: $(1,1), (2,2), \ldots, (6,6)$ — six of $36$. $P = \dfrac16$. Option (a) counts only one doublet.

questions.stem_md: The sum of the probabilities of all the elementary events of an experiment is
questions.solution_md: The elementary events together cover every outcome exactly once, so their probabilities add to $\dfrac nn = 1$.

questions.stem_md: The probability of a sure (certain) event is
questions.solution_md: Every outcome is favourable: $P = \dfrac nn = 1$. (As a percentage, $100\%$ — but a probability is written as $1$.)

questions.stem_md: Three coins are tossed together. The probability of getting exactly two heads is
questions.solution_md: $8$ outcomes. Exactly two heads: HHT, HTH, THH. $P = \dfrac38$. Option (d) treats "0, 1, 2, 3 heads" as four equally likely outcomes.

questions.stem_md: In a game of Ludo, a player needs a 6 to bring a piece out. The probability that she does NOT get a 6 on her next throw is
questions.solution_md: $P(\text{not } 6) = 1 - \dfrac16 = \dfrac56$.

questions.stem_md: A letter is chosen at random from the word INDEPENDENCE. The probability that it is a vowel is

(c) There are no green balls, so $P(\text{green}) = \dfrac{0}{20} = 0$: an impossible event.
